title: Underwear Manufacturing Cost: A Buyer’s Budget
description: Build an underwear manufacturing budget from materials, development, packing and freight. Compare quotes without relying on unverified unit prices.
answer: Underwear manufacturing cost depends on the approved garment, order quantity, materials, labour, branding, packaging and delivery terms. DIYASI lists a 120-piece starting quantity per style and catalogue sample guidance of 5–7 days, subject to the brief; neither establishes a unit price. For a 120-piece order, divide total development and order costs by 120 to compare the effective cost per piece. Obtain a written quotation before choosing a budget, and keep freight, taxes and revisions separate.

sections.title: Define the cost question before requesting prices
sections.text: A useful budget starts with a product definition. A cotton brief, a lace style and a bonded edge design can look like neighbouring catalogue items while requiring different materials and operations. Record the model reference, body composition, gusset composition, construction, size range and colour allocation. Add the exact branding and packing request. Without these inputs, a lower quotation might simply describe a different product. Ask every supplier to price the same brief revision and state which assumptions remain open. Save the quotation date and validity period; a number without those details is difficult to use when the material booking or production date changes. Your first comparison should identify scope differences, before it attempts to identify savings.

sections.title: Separate recurring costs from development costs
sections.text: Create two budget columns. Recurring costs belong to each production unit: fabric or yarn, components, garment assembly, finishing and individual packing. Development costs may relate to pattern changes, artwork preparation, sample construction or testing. The supplier must confirm which charges apply and whether any are credited later. Do not assume a sample fee will be refunded or absorbed into production. A development expense spread across 120 pieces has a different impact from the same expense spread across a larger order. Keep it visible instead of hiding it inside a low headline unit price. For repeat orders, retain the original development line but record whether it actually recurs. This makes the economics of the initial launch and later replenishment understandable.

sections.title: Use catalogue composition as a reference, not a price proxy
sections.text: The DYS201 catalogue reference lists 95% cotton and 5% spandex. LS006 separates its cotton body from a lace component containing polyamide and spandex. These are useful specifications for the request, but composition alone cannot establish cost or quality. Fabric weight, construction, usable width, colour process, shrinkage behaviour and cutting yield may all matter. Ask which of these variables is included in the offer and which needs sample confirmation. Avoid assigning a weight in gsm when none is documented. If a supplier proposes a substitution, request the revised composition, handle, measurements and price together. An apparently small material change can alter fit or wash performance, so an updated quotation does not replace an updated approval sample.

sections.title: Treat branding and packing as their own purchasing decisions
sections.text: A waistband, care label, heat-transfer logo, hangtag, bag and gift box are separate components. They may have separate setup work, minimum quantities and storage implications. Ask whether their quoted quantities match the garment order and who owns any excess components. A retail box can change freight volume even when its purchase cost looks small. Compare a simple launch pack against the intended final retail pack using the same garment specification. Record what is included per unit and what is supplied loose. Check barcode ownership, artwork versions, label language and carton marks before approval. A quotation saying custom packaging is insufficient when your receiving warehouse expects a specific pack ratio or scannable individual units.

sections.title: Compare quantity scenarios without inventing discounts
sections.text: Request alternative quantities only when each scenario is commercially plausible for your brand. The published 120-piece reference is per style; it does not confirm unrestricted mixing across designs, colours or custom components. Ask the supplier to show the accepted allocation for each scenario and quote the same delivery basis. A larger order might reduce some unit costs while increasing cash exposure, storage and unsold inventory. Calculate both total cash required and effective cost per saleable piece. Never fill an empty price tier by extrapolating a percentage discount from another supplier. If the quantity changes the fabric, packing or process, label that offer as a different specification. The decision should reveal the trade-off rather than present a misleading straight price curve.

sections.title: Build a landed-cost calculation with named exclusions
sections.text: A factory quotation and a landed-cost estimate answer different questions. Record the named delivery term and location, then identify transport, insurance if applicable, import clearance, duties, taxes and domestic delivery. Ask a qualified logistics or customs provider to confirm destination-specific charges instead of using a generic percentage. Keep refundable taxes distinct from permanent expenses according to your accountant's advice. Use the agreed shipment quantity for freight allocation and the expected saleable quantity for commercial planning. If you assume rejects, returns or damaged units for a scenario, label the assumption explicitly; it is not evidence of the supplier's defect rate. Keep currency and exchange-rate dates visible so changes in the budget can be explained later.

sections.title: Stress-test cash flow before choosing the lowest unit cost
sections.text: Map payment events against the dates on which money is expected to leave or enter the business. Sample approval, component purchase, production and dispatch may involve different obligations, but no universal deposit percentage is published here. Use the written terms provided for your order. Add freight, inspection and receiving costs at the appropriate stage, then compare the total against available working capital. A reorder that is economical per piece can still be unaffordable before the first batch has sold. Test a slower-sales scenario and a delayed-launch scenario without pretending either is a forecast. Choose a quantity that leaves room to address fit feedback and replenishment. Reducing the number of launch styles may be more effective than negotiating a small unit-price difference.

sections.title: Turn quote comparison into a documented decision
sections.text: Keep one row per supplier and specification revision. Record the unit price, currency, development charges, packing scope, delivery basis, payment terms, sample status and open questions. Mark missing information as pending rather than treating it as zero. Request a corrected quotation when a commercial assumption changes; do not rely on a chat message that contradicts the formal document. Before ordering, reconcile the selected quotation with the approved sample and purchase specification. Explain why the chosen offer fits the launch: perhaps it reduces development risk, supports the required allocation or has a clearer inspection plan. The output of cost research is an auditable purchase decision, not a public claim that underwear can always be manufactured at a particular price.

Total relevant costs and saleable quantity
faq: Is there a published price for 120 pieces?
No verified price ladder is published here. Request a quotation for the exact style, materials, allocation, branding and delivery basis.
Does a higher quantity guarantee a lower unit price?
No. Ask for comparable written offers. Changes in materials, packing or colour allocation can change the economics.
Are sample costs included in production?
Confirm sample charges, revision charges and any credit policy in writing. Do not assume they are included or refundable.
Can this guide calculate import duties?
No. Duties and taxes depend on the destination and product classification. Obtain current advice from your customs or logistics provider.

title: Underwear Manufacturing Process: Buyer Checkpoints
description: Follow an underwear order from specification and samples to production, inspection and dispatch, with approval checkpoints and timing limits.
answer: The underwear manufacturing process runs through six approval stages: brief, material and construction review, sample development, sample approval, bulk production, and final inspection with dispatch preparation. DIYASI's catalogue guidance is 5–7 days for samples and 20–35 days for bulk production, subject to quantity, customization and written confirmation. These are separate planning references, not a guaranteed end-to-end delivery time. Material sourcing, revisions, approvals and freight must be scheduled separately, with a named owner for each decision.

sections.title: Begin with a controlled specification
sections.text: Collect the model reference, drawings, composition, construction details, measurements, tolerances, size range and intended use in one brief. A photograph is useful for appearance but cannot describe every seam, stretch requirement or fit point. State which features are essential and which can use an existing catalogue construction. Give the brief a revision number and keep a change log. When several people approve a launch, nominate one person to consolidate feedback before it reaches the supplier. Contradictory comments create unnecessary sample rounds. Include the destination market and retail presentation so labelling and packing requirements can be discussed early. A complete brief does not eliminate technical questions; it makes those questions visible before time and materials are committed.

sections.title: Review materials and the proposed construction route
sections.text: Ask the team to identify which materials are available, which need sourcing and which require development. Cotton body fabric, stretch lace, elastic and gusset materials should be recorded separately when they differ. Confirm whether the proposed seamless appearance is produced by knitting, bonding or another documented construction; these terms are not interchangeable. Discuss how seams, edges and components affect stretch, comfort and recovery. Request sample evidence for claims such as opacity or wash durability instead of accepting a photograph as proof. Do not write a universal stage duration into the calendar when the material has not been confirmed. The result of this review should be a feasible sample brief with unresolved questions assigned to an owner.

sections.title: Plan the sample round around decisions
sections.text: The published 5–7 day catalogue guidance requires confirmation against the actual brief. Ask what starts the sample clock, whether material is already available and whether the estimate includes artwork or new pattern work. Courier transit is a separate event. Define what the sample is intended to establish: construction, fit, colour, branding or packing. A single sample may not approve every aspect of a production order. If a substitute material is used for an early fit check, mark it clearly so nobody mistakes it for the final approved construction. Keep a list of items that remain unapproved. Arrange feedback promptly after receipt, because time waiting for buyer decisions is part of the real project calendar even when it is outside the factory's work period.

sections.title: Approve measurements and wear behaviour consistently
sections.text: Use the same measurement method for each review. Record whether a dimension is measured flat or stretched, identify the reference points and state the allowed tolerance. Review the intended size set rather than assuming that approval of one size establishes all grading. For fit feedback, record the sample size, relevant body measurements, test conditions and the specific adjustment requested. Avoid vague instructions such as make it more comfortable without identifying the pressure point or movement problem. Keep wash observations separate from initial fitting observations. When the team agrees a change, issue a new revision and confirm whether another physical sample is necessary. The signed approval record should identify exactly which sample and specification authorize bulk production.

sections.title: Release production only after the commercial handoff
sections.text: The published bulk guidance is 20–35 days depending on quantity and customization, but the actual start date and scope need confirmation. Reconcile quantities by style, colour and size with the quotation and component orders. Freeze artwork, care labels, packaging instructions and carton marks. Confirm the payment events and any conditions that must be met before work begins. Ask who is responsible for communicating material or scheduling changes. A requested shipment date is not the same as an accepted production commitment. Put the agreed milestones into a shared order record and distinguish estimated dates from confirmed ones. If a change arrives after approval, review its effect on materials, cost and timing before accepting it.

sections.title: Use incoming and inline checks to catch drift
sections.text: DIYASI's published quality stages include incoming material checks, inline production checks and final inspection. At incoming review, relevant items include fabric condition, colour, elasticity and shrinkage. During production, inspect the construction details that matter to the approved product: stitching, waistband position, gusset construction, measurements and logo placement. The buyer and supplier should agree the evidence to retain, including photographs or measurement sheets where useful. Do not invent an AQL level or imply that a general quality page establishes the sampling plan for your order. Define critical defects and acceptance rules in the order-specific inspection arrangement. The purpose of an inline check is to identify a developing problem while corrective action is still possible.

sections.title: Inspect the finished order and prepare traceable packing
sections.text: Final inspection should connect the finished garment to the approved reference and connect the packed shipment to the purchase order. Check style, colour, size, quantity, label, packing method and carton marks. Confirm how any rejected or reworked units are handled before dispatch. If an independent inspection is required, agree access, timing and the report recipients in advance. Packing lists should allow the receiving team to locate quantities by carton without relying on a verbal explanation. Ask for the final shipment dimensions and weight when arranging transport. An inspection pass and a carrier booking are distinct decisions; neither should be inferred from a photograph of sealed cartons. Keep the release authorization with the order documents.

sections.title: Close the loop after delivery
sections.text: Compare received quantities and labels against the packing list, then record any discrepancy with clear photographs and identifiers. Keep receiving issues separate from later customer fit feedback so the cause can be investigated. For a reorder, document what remains identical and what changes: material, grading, colour, artwork or packing. Reusing the same product name does not guarantee an unchanged specification. Request confirmation of any substitutions and retain a reference sample for future comparisons. Review how long each stage actually took, including your own approval time, without turning one order into a universal lead-time claim. This record helps the next order use a realistic calendar and gives both teams a shared basis for resolving questions.

faq: Can I add the sample and bulk estimates to get a delivery date?
No. Material availability, revision rounds, buyer approvals, inspection and freight must be included separately.
Does one sample approve every size?
Not automatically. Agree which sizes and measurements require review and how grading will be approved.
Is a fixed AQL level included?
No universal AQL number is stated here. Agree the sampling and acceptance plan for the specific order.
What happens if artwork changes after approval?
Ask for the cost, material and timing impact, issue a new revision and confirm whether a replacement approval is required.

title: How to Find a Clothing Manufacturer for Your Brand
description: Qualify a clothing manufacturer with product evidence, a consistent brief, samples and written terms. Use an underwear sourcing example to compare suppliers.
answer: To find a clothing manufacturer, define your product and order constraints, shortlist suppliers with relevant evidence, send the same brief, compare written offers and approve a physical sample before production. DIYASI's underwear catalogue provides a concrete reference of 120 pieces per style, with 5–7 day sample guidance subject to the brief. These numbers apply to its documented underwear route, not to all clothing factories or categories. Use them as questions to verify with each candidate rather than universal industry thresholds.

sections.title: Choose the product family before searching for factories
sections.text: A supplier suitable for a simple cotton brief may not be qualified for a structured bra, technical swimwear or a tailored garment. Describe the construction and intended use instead of searching only for a broad clothing manufacturer label. Identify the skills your product requires: stretch sewing, lace handling, bonding, knitted construction, support components or specialized finishing. Separate essential capabilities from optional future extensions. This prevents a shortlist from being dominated by attractive photographs with no relevant production evidence. If the launch concept is still broad, select one representative product and use it to test feasibility. You can expand the range after the first sourcing exercise has established how the supplier communicates, samples and documents the work.

sections.title: Write a brief that candidates can answer consistently
sections.text: Prepare the same core document for every candidate. Include drawings or a model reference, target composition, size range, expected quantity per style, proposed colours, branding, packing and destination. Explain which specifications are fixed and which alternatives you will consider. If you have a target budget, state the delivery basis and what it includes; otherwise a supplier cannot judge whether the target is realistic. Ask for assumptions and exclusions to be listed explicitly. Give each brief revision a number and use it in the quotation request. When one candidate suggests a material or construction change, evaluate it as an alternative instead of silently changing the comparison for every other candidate.

sections.title: Build a shortlist from evidence you can inspect
sections.text: Look for actual product specifications, original model references, a clear business identity and contact details that remain consistent across documents. A factory page, trade profile or directory listing can help identify candidates, but each is only a starting point. Request evidence relevant to the category and order, such as sample photographs, measurement records or a discussion of the proposed process. Distinguish supplier statements from independent verification. A published capacity number does not establish that capacity is available for your order, and a certificate logo does not prove scope or validity. Record the source and date of each important claim. Prefer a short, relevant shortlist that can be evaluated carefully over a large list assembled from generic search results.

sections.title: Verify who will perform and manage the work
sections.text: Ask whether the contracting business manufactures the product itself, coordinates outside facilities or combines both arrangements. Different operating models can work, but responsibilities should be clear. Identify who controls materials, sampling, quality checks, corrective action and shipment release. Request the legal business details needed for your purchase process and check that payment instructions are consistent with the agreed contracting party. Do not infer ownership of a facility from a video alone. If visiting or commissioning an audit, define the questions it must answer. For a small trial, the most useful evidence may be the consistency of the sample, specification and written response rather than a long presentation unrelated to your product.

sections.title: Compare minimum quantities at the right level
sections.text: Ask whether the minimum applies per style, colour, material, size or custom component. A headline MOQ can hide the constraint that determines the real purchase. DIYASI's published catalogue starting point is 120 pieces per style, while colour splits and branding components require confirmation. Other suppliers may use different rules. Place the proposed allocation directly into the request and ask the candidate to mark any unacceptable line. If the minimum is too high, discuss existing materials, fewer colours or a catalogue-based route before assuming it can simply be negotiated away. Avoid splitting an order across too many suppliers before you understand the added cost of samples, freight, approvals and quality management.

sections.title: Use sampling to test the relationship as well as the garment
sections.text: A sample shows more than appearance. It also tests whether the supplier understands the brief, records changes and responds to specific feedback. Before paying for development, confirm sample scope, charges, expected timing and the handling of revisions. When the sample arrives, compare it against the written request using the same measurement method and documented observations. Ask the supplier to explain deviations rather than sending a general rejection. Record whether the proposed correction addresses the cause. Do not treat a successful sample as proof that every future production unit will be identical; use it to establish the approved reference and inspection expectations. Keep one controlled version of the feedback to avoid contradictory instructions.

sections.title: Score risks instead of chasing a single attractive number
sections.text: A comparison sheet can cover specification match, evidence quality, communication, quantity fit, sample outcome, commercial clarity and delivery planning. Use plain categories such as acceptable, needs clarification and unacceptable rather than pretending a numerical score is objective. Price should sit beside scope and risk. A slightly lower quotation may exclude packing or rely on unapproved materials, while a higher one may still be unsuitable if the minimum order is too large. Document the reason for each decision and the unresolved conditions. If a candidate cannot answer an essential question, keep that item open. The purpose of qualification is to make a defensible choice, not to fill every cell with a reassuring answer.

sections.title: Start with a controlled order and a review point
sections.text: Before production, reconcile the sample approval, purchase specification, quotation, payment terms, inspection arrangement and shipment instructions. Name the person who can authorize changes. Keep the first order narrow enough to learn from it, while respecting the supplier's confirmed minimums. After delivery, review received quantities, construction, labelling, packing and customer feedback against the original goals. Decide whether to repeat, revise or stop the product using those observations. A supplier becomes a reliable partner through documented execution over time; a directory badge or search position cannot establish that relationship. Preserve the records so a later reorder, team member or second supplier can understand exactly what was approved and why.

rows: MOQ by style, colour and component
Quotation, payment, inspection and delivery scope
faq: Should a new brand always choose the lowest MOQ?
No. Compare the full specification, allocation, development costs and your ability to manage the order, alongside the minimum quantity.
Does a catalogue photo prove manufacturing capability?
No. Request relevant specifications, sample evidence and a clear explanation of who will produce and inspect the order.
Can DIYASI produce every clothing category?
This guide does not establish that. Use the documented underwear catalogue; other categories require a specific capability review.
What should I send in the first enquiry?
Send a model reference or drawing, material requirements, quantity by style, size and colour allocation, branding, packing and destination.

title: Seamless Underwear Wholesale: A Sourcing Checklist
description: Compare seamless underwear constructions, catalogue specifications, size allocations and sample checks before requesting a wholesale or private-label quote.
answer: Seamless underwear wholesale sourcing starts by confirming what seamless means for the proposed garment: knitted construction, bonded edges or another reduced-seam design. DIYASI's DYS323 catalogue reference lists an 80% polyamide, 20% spandex body and a 100% cotton gusset in S, M, L and XL. Its catalogue ordering guidance starts at 120 pieces per style, subject to allocation and component confirmation. These facts support a specific enquiry; they do not prove every seamless process, performance claim or ready-stock arrangement.

sections.title: Ask what the seamless description actually covers
sections.text: Buyers often use seamless to describe a smooth appearance under clothing, while suppliers may use it to describe a particular construction. Establish whether the garment is knitted, bonded, cut with reduced seams or assembled using another method. Ask which edges and joining points remain and request close-up evidence of the waistband, leg opening and gusset attachment. Do not assume the absence of visible stitching means the entire garment is knitted as one piece. Record the construction in the specification instead of relying on the marketing name. This distinction affects what needs to be tested during sampling, how repairs or changes can be made, and which supplier capabilities are relevant to the order.

sections.title: Read body and gusset specifications separately
sections.text: DYS323 provides a useful example because the body and gusset are described separately. The body is listed as 80% polyamide and 20% spandex, with a 100% cotton gusset. That information should not be compressed into a single all-over cotton or all-over polyamide claim. Ask for the composition and construction of every material that matters to the wearer. If fabric weight, bonding details or stretch recovery results are unavailable, leave them pending and request evidence. A high stretch-fibre percentage alone does not guarantee a particular level of support, opacity or durability. The approved sample and agreed tests must establish whether the proposed material meets the intended use and retail claims.

sections.title: Distinguish stock wholesale from production to order
sections.text: Wholesale can refer to buying existing stock, ordering a catalogue style for production or developing a private-label version. Ask which route is actually available. A catalogue photograph is not an inventory statement, and a standard model number does not guarantee immediate dispatch. Confirm available colours and sizes, replenishment conditions and whether branding changes require a new production arrangement. If the offer is production to order, use the published timing guidance only after the supplier has checked the brief. If stock is offered, request a dated allocation and clarify how long it can be held. Keep the stock question separate from the manufacturing capability question so neither is answered by assumption.

sections.title: Build the size and colour allocation around demand
sections.text: Start with the documented size range, then request measurements and confirm how the size labels correspond to your target market. DYS323 lists S, M, L and XL; those labels do not establish universal body measurements. Prepare a proposed split and ask whether it is accepted within the per-style minimum. Avoid adding colours merely to make the launch look broad, because each colour may introduce material or production constraints. If you use a planning example such as 120 pieces divided across four sizes, identify it as arithmetic rather than an accepted factory allocation. Review the distribution after real sales or fit feedback instead of assuming an equal size split will be commercially appropriate.

sections.title: Test the garment in the conditions that matter
sections.text: For a smooth-under-clothing product, inspect edge visibility under representative garments and lighting. For comfort, review the waistband, leg opening and gusset during ordinary movement. Record the sample size and fitting conditions so feedback is interpretable. Follow the agreed care instructions during wash checks and document changes in measurements, edges, appearance and recovery. If the garment uses bonded elements, discuss how their durability will be assessed; if it uses a knitted route, focus on the relevant construction and fit concerns. Do not attach numerical performance claims without test evidence. A sample checklist should identify pass criteria before review, reducing the temptation to redefine acceptable performance after a disappointing result.

sections.title: Check whether branding changes the feel or behaviour
sections.text: Heat-transfer logos, care labels and packaging can be appropriate for a seamless collection, but their suitability needs to be confirmed on the actual garment. A transfer can affect stretch or feel, and a sewn label can introduce a contact point that conflicts with the intended comfort position. Ask for artwork dimensions, placement and application method to be included in the sample approval. Review the final care information against the actual materials and construction. Do not assume that an existing logo application used on a cotton style will behave the same way on a polyamide and spandex body. Approve the branded sample, not only the unbranded catalogue garment, when the branding is part of your saleable product.

sections.title: Compare quotes on an identical construction basis
sections.text: Two offers described as seamless underwear may differ in edge construction, gusset material, measurements, pack quantity or branding. Put these details next to the unit price in the comparison. Request the accepted size and colour allocation, sample charges, component minimums, packing scope and delivery basis. No verified seamless price ladder is published here, so the correct next step is a written enquiry rather than a guessed range. If a supplier offers a cheaper alternative, identify exactly what changes and whether another sample is needed. Consider the cost of customer returns or relabelling as a planning risk, without presenting an invented defect rate as fact about any supplier.

sections.title: Prepare a repeatable receiving and reorder process
sections.text: Before dispatch, agree how style, colour and size will be marked on individual packs and cartons. At receipt, compare the goods with the approved sample and packing list, paying attention to construction details that a general appearance check might miss. Keep a retained reference for the first accepted batch. For a reorder, confirm whether the same material and process remain available and whether any colour or component changes require approval. Use actual sell-through and fit feedback to revise the allocation. A wholesale relationship becomes easier to manage when each order references a controlled specification and an accepted sample, rather than a product photograph that may no longer describe the exact garment being supplied.

faq: Does seamless always mean circular knitted?
No. Confirm the actual construction and remaining seams or bonding points for the proposed style.
Is DYS323 made entirely from cotton?
No. Its catalogue lists an 80% polyamide and 20% spandex body with a 100% cotton gusset.
Can I order any size and colour mix at 120 pieces?
The catalogue reference is per style. The proposed size and colour allocation must be confirmed in writing.
Are seamless catalogue styles ready to ship?
A catalogue listing does not prove stock availability. Request a dated stock allocation or an order-specific production schedule.

title: Underwear MOQ Explained: Plan a 120-Piece Enquiry
description: Understand per-style underwear MOQ, size and colour splits, component minimums and trial-order trade-offs before preparing your supplier brief.
answer: MOQ means minimum order quantity, but the unit of commitment matters. DIYASI's published underwear catalogue starting point is 120 pieces per style, not 120 pieces across any combination of styles, colours and custom components. As arithmetic only, 120 pieces across four sizes would average 30 pieces per size; this is not a confirmed production allocation. Ask for the permitted size and colour split, material requirements and branding minimums in writing before using the number in a launch budget.

sections.title: Identify the unit behind every minimum
sections.text: A supplier may specify a minimum by style, colour, fabric, production run or component. These constraints can exist at the same time. Start by asking what the headline number covers and which additional minimums apply. A per-style quantity normally needs a clearly defined design reference; changing the pattern or construction may create a separate style even if the retail collection name stays the same. Ask the supplier to mark the applicable grouping on your proposed order sheet. Do not use a general statement about flexibility as evidence that every combination is accepted. The useful result is an allocation the supplier has reviewed, with the exact quantities and conditions recorded alongside the quotation.

sections.title: Translate a launch idea into an allocation table
sections.text: List each style, colour and size on its own line, then total the quantities at the levels the supplier uses. This simple exercise often reveals that a visually small collection contains many purchasing decisions. For illustration, one style with four sizes has four size positions before adding another colour. An equal split can demonstrate the arithmetic, but it is not a demand forecast or a factory commitment. Use your own customer evidence to propose a practical distribution, then ask the supplier to confirm it. Keep sample quantities separate from bulk quantities. If a requested line is not feasible, ask which changes would make the allocation workable without altering the product's essential purpose.

sections.title: Separate garment MOQ from custom-component MOQ
sections.text: Labels, waistbands, hangtags, bags and boxes may need quantities different from the garment order. Ask whether the supplier can provide the requested component within the launch quantity and what happens to any excess. Record who owns, pays for and stores leftover components, and whether they can be reused for a reorder. A low garment MOQ can still produce a larger cash commitment if the packaging is highly customized. Compare a simple approved packing option with a custom retail presentation using complete costs. Do not assume a published list of branding options proves every option is available at the minimum garment quantity. Confirm component feasibility before treating the launch plan as settled.

sections.title: Understand why material choices change the conversation
sections.text: Existing materials and colours can offer a different development route from custom dyeing or a new construction. Ask what is already available for the specific model and what requires a separate sourcing step. Avoid treating all cotton, lace or seamless materials as interchangeable. Composition, weight, colour, stretch behaviour and construction can affect the garment and the order constraints. If a material substitution is proposed to accommodate quantity, review its effect on fit, feel, care and labelling. Request a new sample where appropriate. The goal is not to force every design into the smallest possible order; it is to choose a feasible specification that still delivers the product your customer expects.

sections.title: Compare fewer styles against a broader assortment
sections.text: A launch with several designs can spread demand uncertainty across more products, but it also multiplies sample reviews, artwork, allocation decisions and inventory positions. Compare a narrow launch using one or two well-defined styles with a broader range using the same total budget. Account for development and packing, not only garment units. A smaller assortment can produce clearer feedback about fit and demand, while a broader assortment may be justified by an existing customer base. Neither option is universally correct. Document the business reason for the assortment and the evidence behind each size or colour choice. Keep room in the budget to respond to the first batch rather than committing everything to untested variants.

sections.title: Negotiate the brief instead of assuming the rule disappears
sections.text: If the proposed quantity is below the confirmed minimum, explain the commercial constraint and ask which alternatives are feasible. Possible discussion points include an existing catalogue model, fewer colours, simpler packing or postponing a custom component. These are options to evaluate, not promises that the supplier will accept them. Request a revised written offer after any change. Be cautious about an answer that agrees to the quantity without explaining which specification or cost assumptions changed. The final order should remain clear enough for both parties to inspect. A concession that produces an undefined garment or surprise component charge is not a useful solution to the minimum-order problem.

sections.title: Use total exposure to decide whether the MOQ is affordable
sections.text: Multiply the confirmed unit quotation by the accepted order quantity, then add applicable development, components, inspection and logistics. Consider the payment schedule and the inventory remaining if sales are slower than planned. Do not interpret a low MOQ as a low-risk guarantee; the product can still be wrong for the market. Likewise, a higher minimum may be manageable for a brand with reliable demand and repeat customers. Use scenarios with clearly labelled assumptions instead of presenting forecasts as facts. The decision should account for how quickly the business can learn, replenish and correct problems. A practical first order supports those activities while preserving enough cash for the next decision.

sections.title: Confirm the reorder rules before the first production run
sections.text: Ask whether a repeat order uses the same minimums and whether retained materials or components affect the arrangement. Confirm the availability and ownership of any leftover branded items. Keep the approved sample, specification, colour reference and artwork version together so the reorder is clearly identified. If a new colour, size or pattern change is introduced, ask whether it remains the same order route or requires new development. Review actual sales and customer feedback before changing the allocation. Record the supplier's current quotation and timing instead of assuming the first order's terms remain valid indefinitely. This turns the MOQ discussion into a repeatable purchasing process rather than a one-time negotiation around a headline number.

rows: Equal split would be 60 per colour
Whether that colour split is accepted
faq: Can 120 pieces cover several different styles?
The published catalogue reference is per style. Do not assume it can be pooled across different designs.
Does 30 pieces per size represent an accepted order?
No. It is the arithmetic average of 120 divided by four. The actual allocation must be confirmed.
Can custom packaging have a different MOQ?
Yes, it may have separate quantity requirements. Ask for the component quantities, charges and treatment of excess materials.
Can I order below the published minimum?
Request a feasibility review for your exact brief. No lower quantity is promised by this guide.

title: Starting an Underwear Brand: A Sourcing Checklist
description: Plan a small underwear brand around a defined customer, controlled samples, complete costs and a realistic first-order allocation.
answer: Starting an underwear brand requires a specific customer and product brief, a qualified supplier, approved fit and materials, a complete cost model, compliant retail information and a controlled first order. DIYASI's catalogue reference starts at 120 pieces per style, with 5–7 day sample guidance subject to the brief. Use those figures to frame an enquiry, not to promise a launch date. Validate one clear product proposition before expanding colours, styles or custom components, and budget for feedback and replenishment.

sections.title: Define the customer problem your first product solves
sections.text: Begin with a concrete wearing situation and a customer you can reach. The product might prioritize an everyday cotton feel, a particular rise, reduced edge visibility or a specific fit preference. Avoid combining every possible benefit into one launch garment. Write down the evidence behind the idea, such as customer interviews, retailer feedback or your own documented product observations. Separate that evidence from assumptions you still need to test. Identify what would make the customer switch from an existing option and how you will show that difference accurately. This decision informs the material, fit, sample checklist, imagery and retail description, helping the sourcing brief remain focused when suppliers suggest alternatives.

sections.title: Choose a manageable assortment and development route
sections.text: Decide whether to start from a documented catalogue model, modify an existing construction or develop a new design. Each route needs different questions and approval work. A catalogue reference can make the first enquiry more specific, but it does not remove the need to review fit, materials and branding. Count the styles, colours and sizes in your proposed assortment and consider how many separate decisions they create. A narrow launch can simplify feedback and replenishment. Do not use a factory's broad category list as a reason to introduce products you have not validated. Bra, shapewear and swimwear concepts require category-specific capability and performance review rather than assumptions borrowed from a brief catalogue.

sections.title: Turn the brand idea into a technical and commercial brief
sections.text: Collect the model reference or drawings, composition, measurements, size range, colour allocation, branding and packaging requirements. State the intended market and any product claims that need evidence. Add the quantity per style and the delivery destination. If some choices remain open, identify the alternatives you want the supplier to evaluate. Include a version number so quotations and samples can refer to the same document. Keep the brand story separate from measurable approval requirements: soft, premium or flattering cannot replace a defined construction and fit review. The brief should allow a supplier to explain feasibility and exclusions without guessing what you mean, and allow your own team to make consistent decisions.

sections.title: Use sample feedback to validate the product promise
sections.text: Agree the sample scope and review criteria before development begins. Check measurements, construction, body and gusset materials, waistband behaviour, leg openings and branding placement. For wear feedback, record the sample size and relevant conditions, then describe specific observations instead of collecting only broad preferences. Follow the agreed care method when checking wash behaviour. If a claim such as invisible under clothing or supportive fit is central to the brand, define how you will assess it and avoid numerical or medical claims without appropriate evidence. Consolidate feedback into one controlled revision. Do not rush to photograph a sample that has not been approved, because the imagery can lock the launch into a construction that later changes.

sections.title: Build a budget that includes learning and selling
sections.text: The garment quotation is only one part of the launch budget. Include sample development, revisions, branding components, packing, inspection where applicable, freight, import costs, receiving and retail operations. Add the cost of creating accurate product photography and information. Keep marketing assumptions separate from confirmed expenses. Calculate how much cash is committed before the first sale and what remains for a reorder or correction. No verified unit-price ladder is published here, so obtain an order-specific quotation before setting margins. Use a slower-sales scenario to test resilience without presenting it as a prediction. A first order should produce useful customer evidence as well as inventory; leave room in the budget to act on that evidence.

sections.title: Prepare accurate labels, claims and product information
sections.text: Confirm the actual composition and care requirements for the approved product, including separate components where relevant. Check destination-market labelling and consumer requirements with an appropriate adviser instead of copying another brand's label. Make size information consistent with the reviewed measurements and explain how customers should choose. Do not add certification logos, sustainability claims or performance statements without evidence that covers the actual product and order. Keep supplier statements distinguishable from independent verification. Review packaging artwork, barcode data and legal business information before approval. The retail page should describe the garment the customer will receive, using original product photographs and clear limits rather than a generalized story that overstates the material or manufacturing method.

sections.title: Plan the launch around approved milestones
sections.text: Work backwards from the desired retail date, but mark it as a target until the supplier confirms the order schedule and logistics are arranged. Catalogue guidance of 5–7 days for samples and 20–35 days for bulk production does not include every approval, revision or transport step. Give each milestone an owner: brief completion, sample feedback, artwork approval, commercial acceptance, inspection and receiving. Avoid announcing an exact delivery promise to customers before the necessary evidence exists. Coordinate photography and store preparation with the approved sample version. Keep a fallback plan for a delayed component or additional fit round, such as reducing the launch assortment rather than accepting an unapproved change simply to protect a promotional date.

sections.title: Measure the first batch before expanding
sections.text: After delivery, compare received goods with the approved reference and verify quantities and labels. Track customer questions, size choices, returns and specific fit observations in a way that protects personal information. Distinguish product problems from unclear descriptions or sizing guidance. Use actual sell-through to plan the next allocation, and review whether the brand's original promise matches customer experience. A reorder can retain the successful construction while adjusting the assortment, but every material or pattern change still needs review. Expand categories only when you can support the added sourcing and quality work. The strongest output of a small first launch is a repeatable product and purchasing process, supported by real customer evidence rather than a larger untested catalogue.

faq: Should a small brand start with many styles?
Choose an assortment you can fund, sample and evaluate properly. More styles create more approval and inventory decisions.
Can I launch within the published sample and bulk times?
Those are conditional catalogue references, not an end-to-end launch promise. Add approvals, revisions, logistics and retail preparation.
Can I use a catalogue model with my own branding?
Request confirmation of the model, branding method, component minimums and sample approval requirements for your order.
What should trigger a reorder?
Use actual demand, fit feedback, remaining inventory and available cash, then confirm current materials, minimums, prices and timing.
